slides.title: Growth Types
slides.notes: Open by treating growth as a measuring device rather than a new algebraic operation. Students already know Cayley graphs and word metrics from earlier chapters, so the new move is to count metric balls and then deliberately forget small-scale constants. Preview the examples because they anchor every formal comparison that follows.

slides.title: Counting Word Balls
slides.notes: Make the distinction between spheres and balls explicit. Sphere size is often easier to see in a tree, but the chapter's growth function is cumulative. This monotonicity matters later when functions are compared up to constants, because a small change in radius should not change the asymptotic class.

slides.title: Coarse Comparison
slides.notes: Explain that coarse comparison is a deliberate loss of information, not imprecision. Exact values depend on the chosen generators and on small radii, but the comparison relation keeps the part relevant to large-scale geometry. This is the same philosophical move as quasi-isometry: ignore bounded errors and linear rescalings, then ask what remains.

slides.title: Changing Generators
slides.notes: Use this slide to connect Chapter 05 with the growth chapter. A new finite generating set may tilt and round the apparent ball shape, but every old step can be simulated by a bounded number of new steps and conversely. The balls nest inside linearly rescaled balls, which is exactly the comparison relation for growth functions.

slides.title: Linear Example
slides.notes: Give students one example where nothing mysterious is hidden in the notation. In the integer group, word length is ordinary distance from zero, so the radius r ball is the interval from minus r to r. The formula also shows why growth is a large-scale statement: changing a few initial values cannot change linear behavior.

slides.title: Quadratic Example
slides.notes: Contrast this example with the line by focusing on spheres. The radius r sphere in the standard word metric is a diamond with four sides, each contributing linearly many points. Summing those linear sphere sizes creates a quadratic ball count, so the visual shape and the formula tell the same story.

slides.title: Exponential Example
slides.notes: Stress that the free group example is not just larger than the lattice examples; it grows by a different mechanism. Reduced words branch persistently because cancellation only forbids one next letter. This creates sphere sizes proportional to powers of three, and cumulative balls inherit the same exponential scale.

slides.title: Diagnostic Plots
slides.notes: Use the generated plot as a diagnostic instrument. On the ordinary axis the free group overwhelms the other examples, while the logarithmic panel turns exponential growth into an almost straight line. The finite data do not prove an asymptotic theorem by themselves, but they train the eye to distinguish polynomial curvature from exponential slope.

slides.title: Polynomial Growth
slides.notes: Present polynomial growth as a constraint rather than merely a slow rate. The line and lattice examples suggest dimension, and more complicated nilpotent examples can have degrees that do not simply equal a visible Euclidean dimension. The key lecture message is that polynomial bounds reveal algebraic organization, not just a small graph.

slides.title: Exponential Growth
slides.notes: Connect the formal inequality to the tree picture. Exponential growth is visible when each layer produces a fixed multiplicative supply of new elements, up to coarse constants. The uniform version is more subtle because it asks whether that supply is robust over all finite generating sets, not just the one used in the drawing.

slides.title: QI Invariance
slides.notes: This is the conceptual proof of invariance, not a line-by-line estimate. The map may distort distances, but only linearly and with bounded error, so an r ball cannot spread beyond a linearly rescaled ball. Bounded geometry controls multiplicity, and the quasi-inverse supplies the opposite comparison. Together these yield equality of growth type.

slides.title: Boundary Diagnostic
slides.notes: Explain why this slide belongs in the growth lecture even though amenability comes later. Ball growth and boundary growth are related ways of feeling the large-scale shape of a group. The square lattice can make boundary small compared with area, while a regular tree keeps producing a frontier comparable to the whole ball.

slides.title: Examples Table
slides.notes: Use the table to consolidate examples without pretending it is a classification theorem for all groups. The table says what evidence to seek: ball shape, sphere-size trend, and robustness under changed generators. Push students to separate a local drawing from an invariant claim by asking whether the clue survives at larger radius.

slides.title: Lab Workflow
slides.notes: Frame the lab as mathematical hygiene. A finite ball can be persuasive, but it can also mislead if the graph has not reached its asymptotic regime. The workflow asks students to predict, compute, visualize, and save a check so the experiment remains tied to an invariant question instead of becoming an attractive isolated picture.

slides.title: Recap
slides.notes: Close by naming the through-line from earlier chapters to later ones. Word metrics made groups into spaces, quasi-isometries told us which large-scale features are meaningful, and growth now supplies a countable invariant of that geometry. The boundary preview should remain in memory because it becomes a natural bridge to amenability.
